blogs.title: Signature Required? Unpacking the ‘Certification’ Mandate in Louisiana’s Insurance‑Premium‑Finance Cancellation Statute
blogs.description: This post dissects the Fifth Circuit’s reading of the term “certifying” in La. Rev. Stat § 9:3550(G)(3)(a). It contrasts the Court’s conclusion—that a handwritten signature is not required—with prior appellate decisions like Benitez v. Elsayed that highlighted missing signatures. By tracing the legislative history and examining how insurers and premium‑finance companies will now structure their electronic notices, the article assesses whether this interpretation closes any loopholes or invites new legislative clarification.

blogs.title: Receipt in the Digital Age: How Email Satisfied Louisiana’s Statutory ‘Receipt’ Requirement in Williams v. GoAuto
blogs.description: Focusing on the Court’s analysis of “receipt,” this entry explores how Black’s Law Dictionary definitions were applied to modern electronic communications. It evaluates why an automated email‑to‑web‑service transmission was deemed sufficient under La. Rev. Stat § 9:3550(G)(3)(b)(i), discusses the broader trend of courts treating digital logs as functional equivalents of physical possession, and predicts how this reasoning will influence other statutes that mandate receipt—especially in insurance, banking, and consumer protection contexts.

blogs.title: When Federal Courts Decline to Certify State Law Questions: Insights from Williams v. GoAuto Insurance
blogs.description: This article examines Judge Southwick’s refusal to certify the disputed statutory interpretation to the Louisiana Supreme Court despite its novelty. It outlines the high threshold set by Jefferson v. Lead Industrial Association for certification, analyzes why appellate courts are cautious about overusing this tool, and considers what this decision means for litigants seeking clarification of unclear state law provisions—particularly when federal courts are forced to resolve substantive state questions without guidance from a state supreme court.
